title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs using 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because baseline validator failures were absent on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. We report the sealed design, deterministic accounting that confirms single shared generation per task, the Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded interpretation of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent→configuration translation with generative language models can increase NetOps productivity but carries operational risk: incorrect or unsafe changes can cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. Whether automated repair materially reduces unsafe changes depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question and ran it under a sealed design: Does an automated deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The paired, shared‑initial design fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if necessary, a single automated repair on that identical candidate. Our contributions are (1) a sealed preregistered paired measurement with full execution accounting; (2) artifact‑grounded reconciliation of how determinism and adapter semantics were enforced and audited; and (3) an operationally focused interpretation of what a degenerate null outcome implies for GVR engineering and evaluation.
sections.related_work: Large literature surveys and empirical studies document LLM factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation proposals include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration translation but generally lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectural proposals and prototypes advocate combining LLM generation with deterministic validators (Batfish‑style checkers) and with guarded agent patterns; independent audits and red teams have documented configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our study is positioned to provide an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and generation policy, addressing a gap where prior work has suggested but not quantified the incremental benefit of validator‑assisted repair under controlled paired contrasts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study preregistration (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test was an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile CIs were computed with 10,000 resamples and bootstrap_seed = 1729. Planning assumptions (baseline ≈30%, target 50% relative reduction) appear in the preregistration and justified the chosen sample size; they did not alter execution decisions.

Task bank, validators, and holdout. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial/final states, workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break), and a required_sequence that the deterministic validator enforces. The primary checker (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) validates syntactic and intent/constraint rules and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal possible validator blind spots.

Adapter semantics and determinism reconciliation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single generation that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. The execution accounting artifacts confirm this enforcement: the recorded hosted model call audit fields show hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, and the deterministic_reconciliation artifact records complete_pair_count = 200 with pair_accounting_consistent = true. Although the model configuration metadata lists the model identifier (gpt‑5‑mini) and a null temperature field, determinism for the confirmatory contrast was achieved by adapter enforcement and single shared invocations per task rather than relying on a specific numerical temperature. We therefore reconcile the apparent inconsistency: the adapter guaranteed single shared initial outputs per task (removing sampling variance), and the reconciliation/audit artifacts demonstrate that behavior.

Repair policy, budgeting, and statistical implementation. When the primary validator reported violations the preregistered policy allowed one automated repair prompt to the same LLM; repaired candidates would be re‑validated. The execution enforcer capped maximum model calls to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs) and enforced the one‑repair‑call budget. The main confirmatory test was an exact McNemar two‑sided test on the 2×2 paired table (n11, n10, n01, n00) produced by the paired analysis executor; bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729. All analysis and seeds are recorded in the archived analysis log.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and outcomes. The run completed all planned episodes and pairs under the frozen plan (completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200). Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task); repair calls used = 0. The primary deterministic validator accepted every initial candidate: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistered repair branch was never invoked because there were no validator failures.

Secondary contamination check. The preregistered Mininet holdout (20 randomized tasks) produced zero validator–emulator disagreements in the executed sample. The contamination summary artifact records zero disagreement flags for that holdout. We disclose a reproducibility gap: the labeled artifact set does not include the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet holdout, which prevents exact bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of the holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count and required_command_count matched and validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true for sampled tasks. Difficulty annotations in the task traces include labels such as "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" and patterns that exercise nontrivial dependency constraints (e.g., make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change), demonstrating the benchmark included deliberately constrained tasks even though the generator outputs satisfied the machine‑checkable constraints under the enforced generation policy.

Missingness and deviations. There were no technical failures affecting primary analysis: missingness_summary records complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. No post‑preregistration design changes or restarts occurred.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate null. The observed null (no validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded empirical outcome: with identical shared initial outputs across conditions there were simply no validator‑detectable failures for the GVR pipeline to reduce. This result does not imply that repair is universally futile; rather it makes explicit that the marginal utility of automated repair depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage for the targeted workload. When baseline failures are rare under a given generator/prompt policy, a single‑pass repair budget produces little marginal safety return for validator‑detected errors.

Design tradeoffs and external validity. The paired shared_initial design intentionally removes sampling variance to isolate the incremental effect of invoking validation and repair on the identical candidate. That internal control comes at the cost of not measuring unconditional failure prevalence arising from re‑sampling or temperature‑driven diversity. Practitioners seeking unconditional operational risk estimates should therefore evaluate alternative designs that include independent per‑condition sampling and multiple draws per task. External validity is further limited by the single tested model (gpt‑5‑mini) and the single repair budget allowed; different models, nonzero temperature sampling, multi‑step repair strategies, or human‑in‑the‑loop escalation could produce materially different empirical outcomes.

Validator coverage and operational assurance. Deterministic validators codify a finite set of syntax and policy checks and therefore can miss device idiosyncrasies or emergent data‑plane failures. The Mininet holdout was intended as an independent end‑to‑end corroborator; its zero disagreements in the executed sample increases confidence for this run but does not guarantee completeness. A practical assurance program should combine richer device models, larger emulation/testbed sampling, and adversarial perturbation testing to probe validator blind spots.

Implications for evaluation and engineering. Before investing in automated repair pipelines, operators should (1) measure baseline validator failure prevalence for their intended generator/prompting policy, and (2) probe validator fidelity using emulation or selective real‑device checks. If baseline failures are rare, resources may instead be prioritized toward expanding validator fidelity and adversarial testing, or toward multi‑sample generation policies that expose latent failure modes that a repair could address.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding an observed paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Because baseline validator failures were absent on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated. The artifact‑grounded outcome makes explicit that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generation policy, single‑call automated repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory work should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity with richer emulation or real‑device checks, evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to quantify practical operational gains. All execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived for independent inspection under the preregistration id cited above.

limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
